title: The Definite Article
lede: A complete revision chapter for deciding whether a noun is definite or indefinite, pronouncing الـ accurately with sun and moon letters, connecting words naturally, and preserving correct spelling in Cambridge IGCSE reading and writing.

items.feedback: ✔ الْكِتَابُ is definite because it begins with الـ .
✔ Arabic has no separate equivalent of English “a/an”. In a fully supported model, tanwīn may also signal indefiniteness.

items.prompt: Which begins with a sun letter?
items.feedback: ✔ ش is a sun letter. The lām sound assimilates and ش is pronounced with shadda.

items.prompt: How should “in the house” be written?
items.feedback: ✔ Write every word fully. Connected pronunciation never licenses phonetic spelling in formal writing.

items.prompt: Which means “the new school” as one noun phrase?
items.feedback: ✔ An attributive adjective matches its noun in definiteness: both words take الـ .

options: No proper name may contain ال.
Do not add ال randomly; some established names contain it.
items.feedback: ✔ Names such as الْقَاهِرَةُ and الْجَزَائِرُ conventionally contain the article, while personal names such as مَرْيَمُ do not.
Both words are indefinite and agree in gender.
The adjective describes the noun inside one definite phrase, so both take الـ .
The indefinite adjective is the predicate: it tells us something about the definite subject.

options: Arabic has no separate word for a/an.
Tanwīn is always written in normal unvowelled prose.

items.feedback: The shadda represents assimilation of the lām to the following sun letter.

items.feedback: ب، ق، م are all moon letters.

items.feedback: د، ز، ص are all sun letters.

blocks: ## Why this matters لِمَاذَا هَذَا مُهِمٌّ؟
The article changes meaning, pronunciation and agreement. One small prefix can decide whether you mean any school, a particular school, a noun phrase or a complete sentence.
### 📖 Read precisely
مَدْرَسَةٌ means “a school”; الْمَدْرَسَةُ means “the school”. The difference can identify the correct person, place or answer.
### 👂 Hear word boundaries
In connected speech, the initial vowel of الـ may not be heard, and the lām assimilates before a sun letter. The written article remains present.
### ✍️ Write accurately
Cambridge writing rewards control. Do not spell connected pronunciation phonetically, and do not add or remove الـ randomly.
[callout] The central decision: Are you naming something generally, or referring to a particular, known or already identified noun?
## Choose your route اِخْتَرْ مَسَارَكَ
Complete the Core route first. Use Develop and Stretch to deepen accuracy rather than rushing through every section at once.
### Recognise and pronounce
- Distinguish definite and indefinite nouns.
- Identify sun and moon letters.
- Keep spelling unchanged in connected speech.
### Build accurate phrases
- Match noun and adjective definiteness.
- Distinguish a phrase from a sentence.
- Apply the article in short texts.
### Control the boundaries
- Recognise article behaviour in idāfa.
- Handle established names containing الـ .
- Explain hamzat al-waṣl precisely.
## Diagnostic start اِخْتِبَارُ الْبِدَايَةِ
Answer before reading the explanations. Your first attempt shows which decisions need attention.
## Definite or indefinite? مَعْرِفَةٌ أَمْ نَكِرَةٌ؟
Start with meaning. The article is not decoration: it tells the reader whether the noun is specific or non-specific.
### Indefinite: one non-specific member
كِتَابٌ = a book / a book of some kind.
There is no separate Arabic word equivalent to English “a” or “an”. In fully vowelled teaching examples, the noun often carries tanwīn.
### Definite: a known or specific noun
الْكِتَابُ = the book.
Add الـ directly to the beginning of the noun. In normal Arabic script it is not separated by a space or hyphen.
[example] بَيْتٌ → a house non-specific
[ar] بَيْتٌ
[example] الْبَيْتُ → the house specific or known
[ar] الْبَيْتُ

[callout] Do not overtranslate tanwīn. Tanwīn is a grammatical ending, not a separate written article. At later stages, final case endings may be omitted in ordinary unvowelled writing even though the noun remains indefinite.
### From noun to noun phrase

TABLE: Meaning | Arabic | What to notice // a new school | مَدْرَسَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ | Both noun and adjective are indefinite. // the new school | الْمَدْرَسَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ | Both noun and adjective are definite. // The school is new. | الْمَدْرَسَةُ جَدِيدَةٌ. | Definite subject + indefinite predicate creates a sentence.
## Sun and moon letters الْحُرُوفُ الشَّمْسِيَّةُ وَالْقَمَرِيَّةُ
The spelling of الـ stays the same. What changes is the pronunciation of its lām before the following letter.
### ☀️ Sun letters: the lām assimilates
ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن
The lām is not pronounced separately. The following consonant is doubled and written with shadda in fully supported text.
الشَّمْسُ → ash-shamsu النَّاسُ → an-nāsu
### 🌙 Moon letters: pronounce al- clearly
ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م هـ و ي
The lām remains audible. In fully supported text it normally carries sukūn.
الْقَمَرُ → al-qamaru الْبَيْتُ → al-baytu
[callout/warning] Important correction: الشَّمْسُ is pronounced approximately ash-shamsu , not “āsh-shams”. The opening vowel is short, and the word is still written with the complete article.
### What exactly changes?

TABLE: Feature | Moon letter | Sun letter // Example | الْقَلَمُ | الطَّالِبُ // Pronunciation | al-qalamu | aṭ-ṭālibu // Lām sound | heard | assimilated // Following letter | normal | doubled; shadda shown when vowelled // Spelling of الـ | unchanged | unchanged
## Hamzat al-waṣl and connected speech هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ وَالْكَلَامُ الْمُتَّصِلُ
The alif at the beginning of the article carries hamzat al-waṣl. It helps start the word, but its vowel is not pronounced when speech connects from the preceding word.
### Start after a pause
At the beginning of speech, pronounce the initial vowel:
الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.
al-baytu kabīrun — The house is large.
### Connect after another word
After a word ending in a vowel sound, the initial vowel of the article is not pronounced:
فِي الْبَيْتِ
fī l-bayti , not a careful word-by-word *fī al-bayti*.
إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ
ilā l-madrasati .
[callout] Writing rule: Connected pronunciation is never an instruction to delete letters. Always write فِي الْبَيْتِ , not فِلْبَيْتِ and not فِي لْبَيْتِ .

[callout] Two processes may occur together. In فِي الشَّارِعِ , the initial vowel of the article is elided because speech is connected, and the lām assimilates because ش is a sun letter: approximately fī sh-shāriʿi .

TABLE: Written form | Careful start | Connected after a vowel | Spelling change? // الْبَيْتُ | al-baytu | فِي الْبَيْتِ — fī l-bayti | No // الشَّمْسُ | ash-shamsu | وَالشَّمْسُ — wa-sh-shamsu | No // الْمَدْرَسَةُ | al-madrasatu | إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ — ilā l-madrasati | No
## Where the article does—and does not—belong مَوَاضِعُ «الـ» وَحُدُودُهَا
The safest rule is not “add الـ whenever English has the”. Arabic definiteness is a system involving articles, names, pronoun suffixes and idāfa.
### Use الـ
- for a specific common noun: الْكِتَابُ
- for a previously identified noun
- on both noun and attributive adjective: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ
- inside established names that conventionally contain it: الْقَاهِرَةُ
### Do not add it mechanically
- to an ordinary personal name: مَرْيَمُ , not * الْمَرْيَمُ
- before a noun with an attached possessive suffix: كِتَابِي , not * الْكِتَابِي for “my book”
- to the first noun of an idāfa: بَابُ الْمَدْرَسَةِ
- to an indefinite noun phrase
[callout/warning] Idāfa preview: The first noun does not take الـ or tanwīn. The second term determines definiteness: بَابُ مَدْرَسَةٍ = a school door; بَابُ الْمَدْرَسَةِ = the school door.
[callout] Proper-name precision: “Do not use الـ with proper nouns” is too broad. The correct teaching point is: do not invent an article. Learn the established form of the name.
## Four-skills application الْمَهَارَاتُ الْأَرْبَعُ
Grammar becomes secure when it carries meaning across reading, listening, speaking and writing.
### 📖 Reading workshop — track known and new nouns

أَسْكُنُ فِي مَدِينَةٍ كَبِيرَةٍ. فِي الْمَدِينَةِ مَدْرَسَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ وَمَكْتَبَةٌ عَامَّةٌ. الْمَدْرَسَةُ قَرِيبَةٌ مِنْ بَيْتِي، وَالْمَكْتَبَةُ فِي وَسَطِ الْمَدِينَةِ. أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ لِأَقْرَأَ الْكُتُبَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.
Notice the information flow: a noun may first appear indefinitely because it is new, then return with الـ because it is now known.
### 👂 Listening studio — hear the article
Teacher/browser transcript:
فِي الْحَيِّ سُوقٌ صَغِيرٌ. السُّوقُ قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْمَحَطَّةِ. أَشْتَرِي مِنَ السُّوقِ الْخُبْزَ وَالْفَاكِهَةَ.
Read it aloud twice: first slowly, then with connected pronunciation. Track moon letters, sun letters and hamzat al-waṣl.
### 💬 Speaking studio — introduce, then refer back
Describe a place near you. Introduce three nouns indefinitely, then refer back to each with الـ .
فِي حَيِّي مَكْتَبَةٌ... الْمَكْتَبَةُ...
- Use one sun-letter noun.
- Use one moon-letter noun.
- Connect a preposition naturally.
- Answer: أَيْنَ الْمَكَانُ؟
### ✍️ Writing workshop — My local area
Write 7–10 connected sentences. Introduce at least three places indefinitely, then refer back to them definitely. Include one definite noun–adjective phrase and one complete nominal sentence.
Save and mark complete Clear
Sketch a local-area map and label at least six places in Arabic. Introduce each place once without الـ , then add a second sentence using the definite form.

On paper, write the heading حَيِّي . Draw or write your response, underline indefinite first mentions once, and circle definite references. Use the checklist above before marking the activity complete.
## Grammar Playground مَلْعَبُ الْقَوَاعِدِ
The games test real grammatical decisions. Replay until the explanation becomes more memorable than the error.
### Misconception 1
Wrong idea: “A sun letter removes الـ .”
Repair: It changes pronunciation only. The article remains written.
### Misconception 2
Wrong idea: “After a vowel, write the article as it sounds.”
Repair: Hamzat al-waṣl affects connected speech; standard spelling is unchanged.
### Misconception 3
Wrong idea: “An adjective never needs الـ .”
Repair: An attributive adjective matches the noun in definiteness.
### Misconception 4
Wrong idea: “Proper nouns never contain الـ .”
Repair: Learn each established name; do not add or remove the article by guesswork.
## Final mastery check اِخْتِبَارُ الْإِتْقَانِ
This check revisits every major decision: meaning, agreement, sun/moon pronunciation, connected speech, spelling and article boundaries.
### Today you can… الْآنَ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ...
- distinguish a non-specific noun from a specific definite noun;
- pronounce الـ with all sun and moon letters;
- explain why the spelling remains unchanged in connected speech;
- match a noun and adjective in definiteness;
- avoid adding the article inside possessive suffixes and the first term of idāfa.
Personal next step: Score below 7/10 — revisit Sections 1–3. Score 7–8 — replay the repair game. Score 9–10 — continue to Articles Lesson 2 on definiteness and adjective agreement.
Spaced revisit: Return in 3–7 days and complete the final check without rereading the lesson first.
